claims.text: The estimated prevalence of user reports indicative of LLM hallucinations is approximately 1.75% within mobile app reviews initially flagged as relevant to AI errors.
Factual Incorrectness (H1) is the most frequently reported LLM hallucination type in AI mobile app reviews, accounting for 38% of confirmed instances.
Nonsensical or Irrelevant Output (H3) accounts for 25% of confirmed user-reported LLM hallucination instances in AI mobile app reviews.
Fabricated Information (H2) accounts for 15% of confirmed user-reported LLM hallucination instances in AI mobile app reviews.

Review snippets describing LLM hallucinations exhibited an average VADER compound sentiment score of -0.65 compared to -0.40 for full reviews and +0.15 for general AI reviews not reporting hallucinations.
Reviews containing confirmed LLM hallucination reports had a lower average star rating of 1.8 stars compared to 3.5 stars for AI reviews without hallucination reports and 3.9 stars overall.
The heuristic candidate identification algorithm achieved a Precision of 0.65, Recall of 0.78, and F1-Score of 0.71 on the 1,000 manually annotated candidate review dataset.

evidence.description: 350 reviews out of 1,000 manually annotated candidates from a candidate pool of 20,000 AI-error filtered reviews were confirmed as hallucination reports, yielding an estimated prevalence of ~1.75%.
Categorization of 350 confirmed hallucination reports showed Factual Incorrectness (H1) accounted for 38% of all identified reports.
Taxonomy analysis of 350 confirmed reports showed Nonsensical/Irrelevant Output (H3) was the second most common category at 25%.
Taxonomy analysis of 350 confirmed reports showed Fabricated Information (H2) was the third most common category at 15%.
VADER sentiment analysis yielded average compound scores of -0.65 for hallucination snippets, -0.40 for full originating reviews, and +0.15 for general non-hallucination AI reviews.
Quantitative analysis of star ratings showed confirmed hallucination reviews averaged 1.8 stars versus 3.5 stars for non-hallucination AI feature reviews and 3.9 stars overall app average.
Algorithm 1 evaluation against 1,000 human-annotated reviews resulted in precision=0.65, recall=0.78, and F1=0.71.

methodologies.name: Heuristic-based candidate prioritization and mixed-methods review annotation framework
methodologies.description: A multi-stage method combining AI-context keyword filtering, hallucination dictionary matching, NMF topic modeling, VADER sentiment scoring, and low rating amplification to prioritize reviews for manual qualitative coding and taxonomy construction.
datasets: 3 million user reviews from 90 AI-powered mobile apps across 10 categories (Google Play Store and Apple App Store)
conditions: Reviews posted between January 2022 and December 2024
Filtered to 350,000 reviews via AI context keywords
Filtered to 20,000 reviews via hallucination indicator dictionary
Stratified random sample of 1,000 top-ranked candidate reviews manually annotated by two researchers (Cohen's Kappa >= 0.75)

limitations.text: User review descriptions of AI errors can be ambiguous and do not typically use technical terminology, introducing potential subjective interpretation during annotation.
Initial keyword filtering and candidate prioritization heuristics may miss hallucination reports expressed in unconventional phrasing or incorrectly flag non-hallucination reviews.
The focus on English-language reviews across 90 apps limits generalizability across other languages, cultures, platforms, or proprietary LLMs.

Evaluations conducted in controlled laboratory settings or synthetic benchmarks fail to capture the full spectrum of hallucination issues or their nuanced impact on everyday users of deployed mobile applications.

future_work.text: Develop and evaluate supervised machine learning models trained on annotated review data incorporating linguistic and sentiment features to automatically detect user-reported LLM hallucinations at scale.
Conduct larger-scale, cross-platform, cross-lingual, and longitudinal studies to analyze how hallucination reporting evolves across LLM model generations.
Investigate specialized in-app feedback mechanisms that directly link user hallucination reports with the specific LLM interaction context for diagnosis.
